In three early drafts the box was simply approached and refused, so two variants would have shared an answer and W3's would have been the thin one. I re-cut slot 3 so the box plays a structurally different role in each variant: refused for authenticity (W1), a temptation toward sweetness (W2), the source of the pitch everything else is retuned to (W3), a flattering part rejected for a durable one (W4), and a shortcut closed under the narrator's hand (W5). RW-S11-5 was second hardest: the child variant (W2) originally ended on a flat handover with nothing for the narrator to have understood, so I gave W2 an equal-weight closing beat (four wrong notes and Vesna's smile) to match W1's photograph, W3's long silence, W4's dated lid and W5's unwrapped return to the loft. In RW-S11-3 the W5 answer was four words short and the only one with no 'since' clause, so it was lengthened and matched. No answer names a proper noun, a street or a date, so nothing can be re-homed by keyword to another variant's passage; 'grille', 'tin box' and 'reed' appear in all five passages equally.

variants.passage:
My aunt Vesna keeps the accordion shop on Vrbnik Street, the one my grandfather opened with a borrowed lathe and a hand-painted sign he made twice, because the first one leaned. I spent July at the low bench under the window, holding parts while she named them. On the bench between us lay the instrument she had promised for the end of the month. It belonged to the town museum, which wanted it upright in a glass case by autumn with a card beside it giving my grandfather's dates. Nobody would ever play it there. The curator had asked only that it look exactly as it had looked in 1931, down to the color of the bellows tape.

"We work for the eye on this one," Vesna said. "A visitor gets four seconds and a pane of glass. Everything anyone will ever know about your grandfather's hands has to survive that." So she matched the old wine-red tape from a bolt she had hoarded for eleven years, and she left the dent in the grille where it had always been, because the photographs showed it.

The instrument lay open the way something lies open on a surgeon's table: bellows folded back, reed blocks lifted out and stood in rows on a square of felt. Vesna worked without hurrying. She kept a chalk line down the middle of the bench, and everything she had touched went to her side of it. I found a reed that buzzed and swapped it for a clean one from the tin box of salvaged reeds on the shelf. Vesna lifted my reed out again, put the buzzing one back, and screwed the block down. "It has to be the reed that was in it," she said. "Nobody will hear it, and I will know." Then she polished the case until the window showed in it. When she carried it to the front room I saw the whole shop reflected in the lid, both of us in it, and I understood that we had spent the month making a photograph.

My aunt Vesna keeps the accordion shop on Vrbnik Street, the one my grandfather opened with a borrowed lathe and a hand-painted sign he made twice, because the first one leaned. I spent July at the low bench under the window, holding parts while she named them. On the bench between us lay the instrument she had promised for the end of the month. It belonged to nobody. It was my grandfather's own, the one he had kept under the counter and never sold, and no customer was waiting and no invoice would be written for it. Vesna had carried it down from the loft in June without saying why, in a week with paying work in it.

"Some work is for no one," Vesna said. "That is the only work that tells you what a workshop is actually for." So she took it slowly and out of order, doing whichever part she felt like doing that evening, and she left the dent in the grille where it had always been, because her father had put it there himself and she could still hear him laughing about it.

The instrument lay open the way something lies open on a surgeon's table: bellows folded back, reed blocks lifted out and stood in rows on a square of felt. Vesna worked without hurrying. She kept a chalk line down the middle of the bench, and everything she had touched went to her side of it. I found a reed that buzzed and reached for the tin box of salvaged reeds on the shelf. Vesna shut the lid of the box under my hand. "Not out of the tin," she said. "I will cut one." It took her three evenings to make a reed I could have fitted in a minute. Then she played eight bars on it, badly, and stopped in the middle of a phrase. She put the instrument back up in the loft without wrapping it, as though she meant to take it down again soon.

Every RW-S12-1 answer now carries the same kind of numeric content (two counts or a level plus a bound) and the same clause shape, and W2's flatness is stated in its passage as a measured six-season result. variants.passage:
For six summers Dr. Ines Varela's crew has climbed the same wet slope on Ketil Island before dawn, pushing a gloved arm into storm-petrel burrows to feel whether a chick is inside. The work is tedious and low-tech: a numbered stake at every burrow, a tally sheet in a plastic sleeve, and, by a rule Varela has never relaxed, a scale for every twentieth chick. Mainland colonies of the same bird have been shrinking for twenty years, so anything Ketil does differently is worth a season of somebody's life.

The tally sheets show occupied burrows climbing from 610 in the first season to 940 in the sixth, and the gain has appeared on every slope the crew works, not on one favored corner. The scale shows something quieter. Chicks weighed at twenty days old average within a few grams of what they did in the first season, year after year, while their numbers grow.

Varela credits water rather than land. Each July a plume of cold meltwater slides out of the retreating glacier in the fjord opposite and runs past the island's north shore, and the crew can see where it lies by the line of glassy water offshore. Plankton crowd the plume's edge, and the small fish that follow the plankton are the fish the adults bring home. In the Julys when the plume runs strongest, the burrow counts and the crew's offshore sightings of feeding rafts rise together.

Ketil's introduced rats disappeared early in the study, and a visiting biologist has argued ever since that their removal is the whole story. Varela will not call that wrong, only lucky: the trapping happened to finish in the same season the plume first ran strong. Next summer she will drop temperature drifters in the channel to see which of the two the counts actually follow.

Varela is careful about what a tally sheet can carry. "Six summers is six summers," she tells students who want a headline. "It is a pattern, not a law."

For six summers Dr. Ines Varela's crew has climbed the same wet slope on Ketil Island before dawn, pushing a gloved arm into storm-petrel burrows to feel whether a chick is inside. The work is tedious and low-tech: a numbered stake at every burrow, a tally sheet in a plastic sleeve, and, by a rule Varela has never relaxed, a scale for every twentieth chick. Mainland colonies of the same bird have been shrinking for twenty years, so anything Ketil does differently is worth a season of somebody's life.

The tally sheets show occupied burrows drifting slowly downward across the six seasons, from 700 in the first to about 665 in the sixth, on every slope the crew works. Varela credits the fishing fleet rather than the island. Forty kilometres east, a squid fleet works through the night under banks of lamps that draw the petrels' prey up into a lit ring at the surface. Birds the crew has tagged now come back to the burrow after two nights away instead of five, and their tracks bend east toward the fleet. A chick fed twice as often, Varela says, is a chick that fledges rather than starves in the tunnel.

Ketil's introduced rats disappeared early in the study, and a visiting biologist has argued ever since that their removal is the whole story. Varela has come round to it: the rise in fledging began the season the last trap was pulled, two years before the fleet moved east. Next summer she will go back through the photographs taken before the study began.

The bus set Iris down at the top of Tarn Row at four o'clock, and she walked the last hundred yards the way she had walked them at nine, counting the iron gates. There were still eleven. She had a sheet of tracing paper folded in her coat, because the kitchen doorframe was to be taken out on Friday, and the pencil marks on it - her height every August until she was twelve - would go with it. The new owner had written back to say she could copy them if she came before the joiners.

The house was smaller than the house she had been carrying. Everyone had warned her about that, and it was true, and it cost her nothing. What cost her something was the plum tree. Where it had stood there was a half-moon of pale gravel, raked flat and wide enough to turn a car in.

Mr. Halloway was in his doorway across the road, twenty years older all at once, and he knew her before she spoke. "You'll have seen," he said, and tipped his chin at the gravel. "He did it in one afternoon. Never asked a soul."

Iris waited to feel what Halloway plainly felt, and it did not arrive. The tree had never been hers, and nobody had promised it to her; she was sorry about it in the ordinary way one is sorry about weather. What she had come for was indoors, in soft grey pencil, and it was still there.

She let herself in, knelt, and laid the tracing paper against the frame. The marks came up faint but whole: 1994, 1995, the crooked one from the summer she had stood on a book. variants.passage:
A millstone does not grind by crushing. Its working face carries shallow grooves, called furrows, that scissor past one another as the upper stone turns, so that the grain is cut rather than mashed. Furrows wear flat within a few weeks of steady work, and a flat stone heats the flour and spoils it. Every mill therefore kept a dresser, or hired one who walked a circuit of the valley: a tradesman who lifted the runner stone, laid it face upward on trestles, and recut the whole pattern by hand with a steel pick.

He worked by ear. Every blow of the pick sent back a note, and a note that returned dull meant soft rock under the surface, which would crumble beneath the first heavy load. An apprentice spent his first year listening to blows he was not permitted to strike, until he could name the depth of a cut without looking.

The trade had its own vocabulary. A dresser spoke of the charge of his pick, meaning the weight of iron packed behind the point, and no one outside the valley mills would have known what was meant.

Thomas Ede dressed stones in the valley mills for forty-one years. The mills fitted steel roller plant in 1878, and rollers ask nothing of a dresser. Ede cut his last stone in 1883 and spent his remaining years mending roads. The rollers made whiter flour and cheaper bread, and it would be foolish to wish them away. Something went out with the stones even so, which no ledger of the change recorded: forty-one years of judgment, gathered one blow at a time, and answering by 1883 a question that nobody in the valley still asked.

The road up to Ivy's had been resurfaced since June, and Nell arrived earlier than she had meant to. Her aunt was already on the back steps with the enamel bowl in her lap and a paper sack of beans beside her, as though she had been sitting that way since the phone call.

"You made good time," Ivy said.

"They finally fixed the washboard stretch."

Nell sat one step below her and took a handful. For a while there was only the small percussion of beans dropping into enamel.

"Six weeks and they'll be done," Ivy said, lifting her chin at the garden. "You'll see the second picking."

"Mm," Nell said — and then she talked. She talked about the detour at the reservoir, about the truck that had sat on her bumper for eleven miles, about the price of coffee at the filling station. Under the sugar tin, on the step between them, lay a long envelope. Nell had put it there herself while Ivy was inside after the salt, meaning to slide it out at the right moment. Inside was a contract with a start date on it, and the date was thirteen days off, and the city printed above it was four thousand miles from this step.

"Warm for August," Nell said.

"It'll break Thursday." Ivy shelled on. "You'll stay past the weekend, anyway."

Nell looked at the gate, which had sagged for years.

"That hinge wants replacing," she said. "I'll do it in the morning, before the heat."

She reached past the tin, took the envelope back, and put it in her bag.

Renna Okoye had watched raccoons along the Ochlockonee for eleven years before she built the box. It was a cube of clear acrylic, forty centimetres on a side, with a single grape resting on the floor where any animal could see the fruit and none could reach it. The lid was held by a brass bolt seated in a channel on the front face. The bolt was under spring tension: it had to be pushed sideways and held there while the lid was raised, since letting go of it snapped it back into place.

Okoye set the box at the edge of the clearing one evening in March, backed into a canvas blind, and started the infrared camera. The young male the station called Tilt arrived at 9:14. He circled the box twice, put his forepaws on the lid, and then went to work. For eleven minutes he pulled at the bolt and let it go, pulled and let it go. Then one paw stayed on the bolt while the other lifted, and the lid came up. He repeated the two-handed opening on his next four visits without a single failure.

A single solved box proves very little, and Okoye knew the objection she would hear. Anyone could say he had memorised a set of motions rather than understood a catch. So Okoye built a mirror image of the box, with the bolt channel running the other way, and put it out on the fourth night. Tilt opened the reversed box in forty seconds.

Okoye now thinks Tilt was working from something like a picture of how the catch behaved, not from a remembered routine, though she is careful to say that one animal opening two boxes is a story and not yet a result. Her next box hides the bolt beneath a hinged flap.

question_parity_note: Hardest to balance was RW-S17-1. In W5 the fault is one of method rather than of the object, and my first draft answered it 'Nothing in the object is faulty...' — the only negative in the set, instantly re-homable in a blind line-up as the odd one out. I rewrote the answer to name a concrete defect in the same grammatical shape as the other four ('The boards were sized from his written figures rather than from the sheets, so nothing was measured by her'), and rewrote W5's second paragraph so Halvard actually asks 'Where did you measure the text block?', making the mis-sourced measurement a fault he identifies, parallel to grain, stations, gold and paste. RW-S17-4 also needed engineering: it turns on a comparison in the final paragraph, so every variant carries one figure of equal weight and identical placement (seed / road / signature / handwriting / lamp) and none is more vivid than the rest. RW-S17-3's five answers are forced into 'It shows him ...ing ... so ...' so no answer can be chosen for sounding more like an explanation; Q2 answers are all bare 'that' clauses of 16-18 words; Q5 all 22-word 'An apprentice learns that X, and that Y'; Q6 all verb-initial predictions of 17-20 words. Reading each set with no passage, I cannot rank them: each names a specific craft fact and a specific consequence, and no set contains a both/and reconciling option — the five readings are mutually exclusive rather than nested, so the 'most balanced' heuristic has nothing to grip. Passages are 340-343 words (1% spread) and share every word outside the three slot spans.

The shop smelled of wheat paste and old leather, as it had every morning for the two years Ines had been Halvard's apprentice. She had swept it, cut boards for it, and pared leather so thin that the window showed through it, and in all that time she had not been allowed to bind a book from start to finish. On Thursday Halvard had set a stack of folded sheets on her bench and gone out without saying anything, which was how he gave permission.

She worked four days. When she put the finished book on his bench on Friday evening he did not pick it up at once. He wiped his hands, moved the lamp, and turned the book over with one finger, the way he turned everything, as though it might be asleep.

"You cut the boards across the grain," he said. He let one cover fall open and closed. "It will lie flat this month. By next winter it will cup like a leaf and pull at the joint." Ines could feel it now that he had said it, the fibres running the wrong way under her thumb.

He did not make her take it apart. He set the book on the high shelf by the window, where the sun came in hard after noon and the damp came up in spring. "Leave it there," he said. "I could tell you what happens, and you would believe me. That is not the same as knowing." Then he went back to his own sewing frame.

Ines looked at the book every morning after that, and for a long while nothing happened at all. The waiting was its own instruction, like a seed pushed into cold ground, which answers no question until the season answers it. In March the cover began, very slightly, to lift at the fore-edge, and she found that she was not disappointed. She would let it finish, she decided, and cut the next boards with the grain, and never once need to be told again.

Ines sewed until the lamp guttered, beginning again at the fault rather than at the place where it showed. Undoing was the trade's real lesson, she thought, like a road walked back to the turn that was wrong, since no distance gained past it counts for anything. By two in the morning the block held firm at five stations. She would not save an hour again, she decided, on anything meant to be opened by somebody not yet born.

In the spring of 1903 the harbor commission of Alder Cove, a fishing port of nine hundred people, met to settle a question it had deferred for six years. Hollis Vane, the engineer the town had hired the previous autumn, laid his plan before the seven commissioners: to dredge the inner channel to a depth of eighteen feet, so that loaded vessels could reach the sheds at any state of the tide. His estimate was fourteen thousand dollars, more than Alder Cove had ever borrowed at one time. When the meeting opened, the standing motion was the merchant Amos Kerr's, to table the question until the following spring. Two commissioners, Pell and Danforth, had said nothing at all.

What moved them was neither Vane's drawings nor his figures. A letter arrived from the marine insurers at Boston, promising that premiums on vessels berthed at Alder Cove would fall by a fifth once the channel carried eighteen feet. Every owner in the room could do that arithmetic, and Pell and Danforth voted with Vane that evening.

Kerr's answer was not that the work was useless. It was that the insurers had promised nothing anyone could hold them to, and would lower their premiums or not as their own ledgers dictated, dredging or no dredging. He lost, five to two, and the town borrowed in June.

The dredge worked through that autumn. By 1907 the channel had shoaled to twelve feet again; the river carried down more than Vane had allowed for. The town borrowed a second time, on worse terms, and dredged the same water over. Premiums fell, briefly. What Vane had sold as a work proved to be an expense the town would carry forever, and the first bill was the smaller one. Vane left in 1908 for a larger post, and the minute book gives the whole business one line.

Inside the oilcloth was her father's ledger, every page of it filled with what he had borrowed from the Ganns across the water. He had died owing it. Marta had spent four years earning the balance, and she was carrying the book over to be marked closed in front of them.

"Sit forward," he said. "Boat's tender."

question_parity_note: The hardest question to balance was RW-S20-3, the vocabulary item. A single fixed word had to carry a genuinely different and equally ordinary sense in all five worlds, which meant the cost paragraph in each variant had to be built around a natural home for that sense rather than the sense being bolted onto a fixed sentence: apprentices drawn into the engine house (attracted), gallons drawn from the millpond (extracted), objection drawn from the skippers (provoked), a steady wage drawn by eleven men (received), interest drawn by a note (accumulated). Two changes were forced by this. W4 originally used 'drew' twice ('the ninety at the racks drew none'), which left the tested word ambiguous; the second use was rewritten to 'were simply not called back'. W2's answer to RW-S20-2 originally read 'drawn down to supply the compressor', which planted the tested word in an option and would have tipped that item; it now reads 'emptied four feet down'. Proper nouns were also stripped from every answer (the millpond, the barrel yard, the note) and replaced with paraphrase, so a keyword matcher cannot re-home an option onto another world's passage. Second-hardest was RW-S20-6, the counterfactual: W3's first draft ended 'and still had no way to sell them beyond the wharf', which is W2's territory and would have re-homed; it was rewritten to 'still had five idle months every year', which is the true inverse of W3's own slot. Reading each option set with no passage, the five members of every set are the same grammatical shape, name a figure wherever any of them names a figure, and hedge to the same degree; none reads as the balanced both/and proposition, because each is simply the flat truth of a different world.

variants.passage:
Havermouth, Maine, had shipped fish for eighty years before it had any way to keep them. The schooners came in on the tide, and whatever the crews could not sell on the wharf by evening went into salt or went to the gulls. In April 1911 the town raised the money, bought a compressor from a firm in Portland, and opened an ice plant at the head of the pier. By midsummer the plant was making twelve tons of ice a day, and Havermouth's fish began to travel.

The change the ice made was in the length of a trip. Before the plant, a schooner had to turn for home on the second day, whatever the fishing. With ice in her hold she could stay out nine days, and the average catch landed at Havermouth rose from eleven barrels a trip to thirty-four.

The cost fell first on the barrel yard. Salt fish had needed tight casks, and Havermouth had kept nine coopers and their apprentices busy the year round. Iced fish went out in cheap slat crates milled up the river. Within four years the plant drew the yard's last apprentices into its engine house, and the cooper's trade was gone from the town.

The town's records, kept through the plant's tenth year, show what the trade came to. In 1921 the six men who owned schooners reported incomes four times what they had earned in 1910. Wages for hired crew stood where they had stood, at eighteen dollars a month and a share. The plant had made the port richer without making most of its people richer, and the town meeting of that year argued about little else.

The compressor ran until 1946, when a larger plant at Beal's Point replaced it. By then no one in Havermouth could remember shipping fish any other way.

The schooners came in on the tide, and whatever the crews could not sell on the wharf by evening went into salt or went to the gulls. The advantage Havermouth had bought was gone in nine years, while the note it had signed ran twenty more. The lead was real, and nobody on that coast could keep one for long.

The compressor ran until 1946, when a larger plant at Beal's Point replaced it. By then no one in Havermouth could remember shipping fish any other way.

For twelve years the light in Mr. Halloran's garage came on at six and went off at nine, and for most of them I watched it from the window over our stairs. He never shut the door while he worked. From the pavement you could see the ribs of a small wooden boat on trestles, and Mr. Halloran moving among them in the same grey cardigan, holding a plane, or a rag, or nothing at all.

He was in no hurry. I once heard him tell the postman that a boat you finish is a boat you are then finished with, and he said it as though it were an ordinary thing to want. Every night at nine he drew a tarpaulin over the hull, as carefully as if the covering, and not the boat, were the work.

My mother said he was lonely; my father said he was busy. Between nine and eleven I preferred my father's account, because it let me go on watching without feeling that I ought to do anything.

The summer I was eleven I crossed the road and stood in the doorway. He put a block of sandpaper into my hand and turned back to the stern. We worked for an hour without speaking, and the only thing he said was "slower," twice. When the light went I was sent home with no more ceremony than that.

After that I watched from the pavement instead of the stairs. I went away to school and then further away, and came back at Christmas and in August. Each time the boat looked to me exactly as it had, and each time, I understand now, it was not.

The spring I turned twenty-one he moved to a flat by the river, and the house was sold with the boat still in the garage, her seams unsealed, a hull that had never touched water and never would.

The window over our stairs looks onto a garage door that stays shut. I still check it at six.

variants.passage:
For fifty-eight autumns, volunteers at Culver Point have counted the hawks that cross the headland on their way south. They work from a wooden platform on the bluff, in four-hour shifts, tallying each bird by hand on a paper card. The resulting archive is one of the longest continuous records of raptor migration on this coast, and the Ridgeway Trust has used it to argue that three species are in decline.

In 2019 the Trust mounted an automated radar unit twenty metres from the platform. It was expected to confirm the hand counts. It did not. Across the first season the radar reported roughly a third more birds than the counters did, and the excess was not spread evenly: on cool September mornings the two records nearly matched, while on the warm afternoons late in the season the radar ran far ahead of the platform.

Neither instrument was obviously broken. Both had been serviced that summer; the volunteers were experienced, and several had counted for more than twenty years. The Trust spent two seasons on the question, pairing the two records hour by hour and sending an observer aloft in a light aircraft on eleven afternoons to see what each machine was seeing. The flights settled it. On warm afternoons the hawks climbed on warm air to eight hundred metres and beyond, where a bird is a speck or nothing at all to someone looking up from a bluff. The radar still registered them; the platform could not. The counters had never been counting the whole migration, only the part that passed low enough to see.

The Trust did not treat the archive as an error. It measures low passage faithfully, and it has measured the same thing for fifty-eight years. What changed was the label: the series is now published as a count of low-flying migrants rather than of migrants, and the decline it reports is a claim about that narrower quantity. The two instruments, the Trust concluded, answer two different questions.

For six years the nursery beds behind the Ferndale field station produced two very different crops of paper-bark hazel. Seedlings in the west beds grew fast and bushy; those in the east beds stayed short and thin. Staff had proposed four explanations, and each had its defenders: the west beds caught more afternoon sun; they had been dosed years earlier with mycorrhizal fungi; they were watered on a different schedule; and an old hedgerow sheltered them from the valley wind. Dr. Talia Renko argued that the four were not equally easy to check, and that one of them could be isolated in a single season. In April she chose that one.

Renko's target was the fungi. She potted one hundred and twenty hazel seedlings in sterilized soil and split them into halves of sixty. Into each treatment pot she stirred a tablespoon of ground root taken from the west beds, still carrying living fungal threads; each comparison pot got the same tablespoon of the same ground root after an hour in a hot oven, which killed the fungi and left the material otherwise unchanged. Both halves stood on one gravel bench in full sun, drew from a single watering line, and sheltered behind the same mesh screen.

Ten weeks later most of the measurements were dull. Stem height, leaf count, and stem thickness differed between the halves by less than four percent. Root mass did not: the treatment seedlings carried roots ninety percent heavier than their counterparts. What Renko called the clearest sign, though, was not a number. Through the two rainless weeks of August, the treatment seedlings went on adding growth, while the comparison seedlings stalled and put out nothing at all.

Dr. Femi Aluko raised an objection Renko had not anticipated. The two halves were not the same age: the treatment seedlings came from a nursery batch germinated three weeks before the batch she compared them with. Matching ages had not occurred to her. Matching pots had — every pot held four liters — and every seedling went into its pot on one April morning, and a technician who did not know the groupings read every ruler. Renko granted the objection its force. Next April she will run the trial again with seedlings germinated on a single day.

Until then, she says, the west beds keep their secret, and three of the four explanations stand untested.

In the spring of 1802 the council of Kirrholm, a river town of about two thousand people, took up a question it had put off for eleven years: whether to replace the rope ferry across the Vess with a stone bridge. The ferry was old and cheap. The bridge would cost more than the town's whole yearly revenue, and the money would have to be borrowed from a banking house in Reval. The recorder, Petra Lund, left four pages of minutes that give the hour of adjournment and the tally but not the arguments; what the council actually weighed has had to be reconstructed from the letters its members wrote that summer.

That spring a grain house in Riga offered Kirrholm a five-year contract on terms nobody in the town had seen before: delivery in winter as well as summer, at a fixed price. Loaded wagons could not cross on a rope ferry in February, and the contract was worthless without a crossing. Lorens Falk, the engineer the council had hired in 1799, laid before the members a survey of the riverbed showing where piers could stand and what weight the roadway would bear. It was Falk's survey that made the merchants' promise sound like arithmetic rather than hope.

The chamber had been divided since 1791, and the division was about money. Margit Aden, who held the chair, had promised her neighbours that she would not raise the hearth tax. On the second day she proposed that the Reval loan be serviced entirely from tolls collected at the bridge itself, so that no household would pay for a crossing it did not use. Four members who had voted no for a decade said that the objection had never been to the bridge. The measure carried seven votes to five.

The grain house failed in 1806 and the winter contract lapsed after three seasons. The tolls, however, were paid not by grain wagons but by carters, drovers and travellers whom nobody in 1802 had thought to count, and the Reval loan was cleared in 1812, two years early. The reason given for the bridge did not survive the decade. The bridge did, and paid for itself out of traffic that had never been argued about in the chamber.

Lund's minutes preserve none of the arguing. They give the hour the council rose, half past eight, and the tally, and nothing more.

Every weekday for eleven weeks, Dr. Imani Rowe left unmarked envelopes on the paving stones of a busy transit plaza and waited to see what strangers would do. Each envelope held a blank card and nothing of value. A staffed lost-property kiosk stood about twenty metres away, and Rowe's team counted an envelope as returned only if it reached that counter within the hour. Field studies of this kind trade the tidiness of a laboratory for the messiness of real behaviour, and Rowe accepted the trade willingly. Across 1,200 drops, the plain envelopes came back 38 percent of the time.

Rowe's interest lay in a single change. On half of the drops, a small convex mirror was clamped to the face of the kiosk, angled so that anyone stooping to lift an envelope caught sight of their own face. Under that condition returns climbed to 61 percent, a gap far larger than the weather, the hour, or the density of the crowd could account for. Rowe argued that the mirror worked on self-image: a person made briefly conscious of himself as the one acting will act like the sort of person he already believes himself to be, whether or not anybody else is watching.

Dr. Tomas Vance, who studies pedestrian movement, was unconvinced. His objection was not that Rowe's numbers were wrong; he accepted every one of them. It was that the mirror was the brightest object in a grey square, and that it pulled the eye toward the kiosk itself, so that finders handed envelopes in because they had just been shown where to take them.

The two designed a joint follow-up for the next spring, nine hundred drops in the same plaza, arranged so that their explanations predicted different results. One arm kept the mirror. The other replaced it with a frosted panel of the same size and shine, equally conspicuous but showing no face at all. The frosted panel produced 39 percent, indistinguishable from bare paving, while the mirror again produced 60. Vance called the outcome decisive and said so in print.

Rowe has become careful with the word why. The plaza gave her a number that almost anyone could go and reproduce; what it never handed over, she says, was the reason underneath it.

For eleven days Ivo had been making a hare. It was to stand on the ridge of the Marchetti farmhouse: copper, hammered hollow, its ears set back as though it had just heard something move in the grass. On the twelfth morning he carried it up the stairs from the bench room, set it on Mrs. Hallam's table in the front shop, and put his hands behind his back so that she would not see them shaking.

She did not touch it at first. She walked around the table twice, the way she walked around a horse, and then she carried the hare to the window and held it up against the grey light of the yard. Petra, who had been four years with Mrs. Hallam and was allowed now to letter the invoices, went on ruling her lines and did not look up, which Ivo understood as a kindness.

"Here," she said at last, and turned the hare over so that the underside of the shoulder came into the light. The seam there was bright and a little beaded, run fast and hot in one pass. "You closed this in a single breath. It looks well this morning. It will look well next June. In the third winter the water will find the places where you did not wait for the metal to come up to you, and this shoulder will open like a seed pod."

Ivo asked whether he might carry it down again and open the seam and run it a second time, slowly, before it went anywhere. Mrs. Hallam said no. She wrapped the hare in sacking, wrote Marchetti, ridge, north face in the ledger, and stood it by the door for the carter, who came at ten. "It goes up as it is," she said. "The roof is a better teacher than I am, and it is slower, which is the whole of its advantage."

When she had gone out to the yard, Petra put down her pen. "She sent my first three up exactly as they were," she said. "Two came back inside four years. variants.passage:
Ines Vargas had climbed to the limestone plateau above Sarnia Bay for six years before she admitted that she did not understand the plant she had come there to study. The shrub is a knee-high thing with grey leaves and pale, trumpet-shaped flowers, and it opens only after dark. It does not open every night. Her first notebooks record what looks like a rhythm — three nights shut, one night of open flowers — and for two seasons she took the plant to be keeping a calendar of its own.

Then two storms crossed the plateau inside a single week and the shrubs opened on consecutive nights, breaking the rhythm outright. When she went back through six years of her own records, the pattern was plain: the flowers opened on nights that followed a day in which more than four millimetres of rain had fallen, and on no others.

A pattern is not a reason, so Vargas set out to learn who was visiting. She dusted the throats of forty flowers with fluorescent powder and walked the plateau after midnight with an ultraviolet lamp. The powder turned up on the long, scaled tongue of a hawkmoth that hovered at each flower without settling, and on nothing else she caught that season.

Hawkmoths on the plateau pupate in the shallow soil beneath the shrubs, and the pupae cannot force the crust above them until rain has softened it. A flower opening on a dry night would be opening to nobody. Vargas has never watched a moth break the surface, and next season she means to sink funnel traps over patches of bare soil and empty them through wet weeks and dry weeks alike.

What she will claim is narrow, and she thinks it is more useful for being narrow. The plant is not counting nights. It is reading the same signal its one visitor reads, and it is reading it a few hours earlier.

variants.passage:
Ferrow Bank is a low mound of turf and shell sand on the north shore of the Cluvie estuary, dry at spring tide and too small to interest anyone but the sheep that graze it. For eleven summers a team led by Dr. Ines Calvo has taken it apart a trowel-width at a time. Under a collapsed roof of driftwood they reached a floor of packed clay, and on the floor lay four shallow tanks lined with stone slabs, their inner faces still crusted white with salt, and, tipped against the wall, a drift of small fish bones, tens of thousands of them, every fish beheaded in the same manner.

The floor held charcoal as well, and charcoal can be dated. Twenty-six samples went to the laboratory at Ardnave. The results came back in one bundle. Every date falls inside a span of roughly thirty years in the twelfth century, and not one sample sits outside it. Calvo takes this to mean that the mound was worked hard and steadily by a single community and then given up altogether, rather than visited whenever the shoals happened to be good.

Professor Dermot Halloran, who has excavated four comparable mounds on the far shore, reads the same floor differently. The tanks, he argues, were not for salting a catch at all but for soaking hides in seawater before the tanner's work began; on his own sites, tanks of just this shape stand beside pits of lime. The fish bone, he says, is later kitchen rubbish thrown into an empty ruin, and proves nothing about what the tanks once held.

Calvo does not brush the objection aside. She says the question is one that a measurement can decide. The slabs are porous, and porous stone keeps what soaked into it. A specialist at Ardnave is testing the linings for the fatty residues that oily fish leave behind and for the tannins that soaking hides would leave instead. One or the other will be there, and the two do not resemble each other. The results are not yet in.

Neither archaeologist expects the mound to be generous for much longer. The sea has already cut into its seaward side, and what the estuary takes it does not give back. Two summers remain in the excavation permit, and both will be spent in the strip nearest the water, where a shallow channel cut in the clay runs out of the last tank and vanishes into the eroding face; if that channel carried brine down to the sea, the tanks were emptied and refilled many times over.

For eleven summers a team led by Dr. Ines Calvo has taken it apart a trowel-width at a time. Under a collapsed roof of driftwood they reached a floor of packed clay, and on the floor lay two dozen fired clay loom weights in a line where an upright loom had toppled, a scatter of spindle whorls, and, in a waterlogged dip beside them, a wad of unspun fleece still greasy to the touch.

The mound, he argues, was not a workshop at all but an ordinary dwelling; weaving gear turns up on the floor of every house he has dug on the far shore, six or eight weights at a time, and nobody calls those houses factories. The quantity here, he says, is a little larger and nothing else, and proves nothing about who worked there.

Calvo does not brush the objection aside. She says the question is one that a measurement can decide. Loom weights wear where the cords run over them. A specialist at Ardnave is measuring those grooves under a microscope against weights from houses of the same century. Cords rethreaded a few times a year cut shallow; cords rethreaded daily cut deep, and the two do not resemble each other. The results are not yet in.

Neither archaeologist expects the mound to be generous for much longer. The sea has already cut into its seaward side, and what the estuary takes it does not give back. Two summers remain in the excavation permit, and both will be spent in the strip nearest the water, where the waterlogged dip that preserved the fleece runs on into the eroding face; if more fibre survives in it, the range of wools and plant threads worked on the mound can at last be established.

slots: OPENING HOURS AND TARGET AUDIENCE (paragraph 1: when the cooling rooms were open, how they were publicized, and which residents the pilot was built around)
WHAT THE BASELINE COMPARISON SHOWED (paragraph 2: which count moved, by how much, and which count did not)

question_parity_note: Hardest to balance was RW-I17-3, the objection question: the four cautions are different KINDS of objection (a milder month, a mid-summer recoding, a simultaneous alert system, and near-zero attendance), and in a first draft the weather objection read as the 'textbook' answer while the attendance one read as an anecdote. Three changes fixed it. (a) Every objection now carries one concrete quantity of the same grain — four days above thirty-two degrees, a July recoding of one class of stays, alerts sent the same summer, fewer than a dozen weekend visitors — so no answer is the only specific one. (b) Every variant's paragraph 3 runs the identical rhetorical frame, 'Until X, she argued, nobody can say which of the two produced the N percent,' so no variant's caution is stated more decisively than another's. (c) The council sentence in every variant begins 'The council agreed with her and...' and names one funded action, so RW-I17-4 cannot be answered by spotting the only variant where the council actually did something. RW-I17-5 was also re-cut: W1's pilot hits exactly the group it aimed at, which made its answer the only unhedged one in the set, so all four answers were rewritten to the shape 'It appeared in the ___ the pilot was built around, and ___' — W1's second clause ('and in no other age group in the records') is now as qualified as the mismatch answers. Reading each question's four answers with no passage, none is longer, more numeric or more balanced-sounding than its siblings; the surviving differences are which fact is asserted, not how strongly.

variants.passage:
Ferrand has never thought of itself as a hot city, but for nine consecutive summers its public hospital has logged an August spike in patients treated for heat exhaustion. In 2021 the municipal health office, led by Dr. Mireille Okonjo, tried to interrupt the pattern with a pilot it called Open Doors. Six branch libraries were fitted out as cooling rooms, with chilled water, fans, and staff trained to recognize the early signs of heat illness. The rooms opened in the evening and stayed open until nine, on the reasoning that an apartment is hottest well after sunset. The office asked every elementary school in the city to send the schedule home in backpacks, because the pilot was built around families with young children, the group Okonjo believed least likely to have air conditioning at home.

The office had a way of checking whether Open Doors worked. Every heat-exhaustion case at the hospital is recorded with the patient's age, home district, and hour of arrival, and the records reach back far enough to build a nine-year baseline. Okonjo compared August 2021 against that baseline. Visits by children under twelve fell twenty-one percent below the nine-year average. Adult visits did not move: the adult count for August 2021 sits within a single case of the baseline. The whole of the improvement was concentrated in one age group.

Okonjo was the first to say that the number is not yet an argument. August 2021, she pointed out, was mild, carrying four fewer days above thirty-two degrees than the baseline average, and in a cool month emergency visits fall on their own. Until Open Doors has been tried in a hot August, she argued, nobody can say which of the two produced the twenty-one percent. The council agreed with her and voted to repeat the pilot unchanged for a second summer, spending nothing new and waiting for the weather to cooperate. Ferrand's August records will be read again next year, and this time the health office knows what it is looking for.

We had been three days at my grandmother's house on Cardigan Street, and by Sunday afternoon there was almost nothing left to argue over. Nell had gone into the care home in March without ceremony, the way she did everything. My mother, Beatriz, had labelled the last of the crockery and was resting on the bottom stair when I prised the tin box out from under it. Nell had marked every other box in the house in her square capitals. This one carried nothing at all.

Inside were letters, some sixty of them, folded into envelopes addressed in Nell's hand to Ottilie Barr at an address in Trieste. Not one carried a stamp. The earliest was dated 1969, the last the winter before her stroke. She had written about weather, about the neighbour's dog, about my mother's wedding in a green registry office. The envelopes were sealed. She had labelled the linens and the tax files and the photographs; she had labelled everything she expected another person to open.

My mother read two of them standing up, then folded them back along their creases and retied the ribbon. "They're not ours," she said. When I asked who Ottilie was she said she had no idea and did not want to speculate in a house we were already emptying, and she carried the tin out to the car herself, as though I might read more of it.

I decided on the drive back that I had learned something unkind about my grandmother: that she had spent forty years composing a friendship she was too cautious ever to risk posting. It seemed to me the exact shape of her, the words written, the stamp never bought, the envelope sealed against the possibility of an answer.

On Tuesday I sat with Nell by the window and asked about Ottilie. She said the name easily. "She died in the spring of 1971," she said. "Pleurisy. I was in the second year of writing to her by then." She looked at me to see whether I understood, and I did, late. The letters had gone on for forty years to a woman already gone, and the stamp was the only part of it that would have been a lie. The engineer it hired, Dita Okoye, spent her first week on the creek bank rather than at a drawing board. The question was debris. Sedge Creek drains a wooded watershed, and twice in twenty years a storm has sent whole trunks down it at the height of the old deck. A hydrologist's memo put the odds of another such flood inside the bridge's life at better than even. Whatever crossed Sedge Creek would have to take a strike and stand.

How the deck would feel underfoot, which the committee had argued about across two meetings, decided nothing: every option could be built stiff enough that no one would remark on it, and Okoye struck comfort from her comparison matrix. In 2019 Bellhaven stopped charging fares on its buses. The decision was unusual enough that Renata Oyelaran, an economist who studies transport pricing, spent the next four years measuring what it did. Her study tracks every route in the network from 2018 through 2021 and sets Bellhaven beside Corran, a city of similar size forty miles east that left its fares in place.

Ridership in Bellhaven rose thirty-one percent over the two years after the change, and the gain was spread evenly across weekdays and weekends.

The harder question was where those trips came from. Matching boarding counts against travel diaries kept by 2,400 households, Oyelaran found that most of the additional trips replaced journeys people had previously walked or cycled, nearly all of them under a mile; car trips into the city barely moved.

Corran is what complicates the picture. Over the same two years, with fares unchanged, Corran's ridership rose twenty-seven percent on its own. A manufacturing expansion had added jobs on both sides of the county line, and Oyelaran's estimates leave regional employment growth, rather than the removal of the fare, doing most of the work in Bellhaven's figure.

She is careful about what the numbers license. Cities weighing a fare-free policy, she writes, should not take Bellhaven as evidence for one, since nearly all of its increase would have arrived regardless.

Not everyone accepts the reading. Oyelaran answers that dropping the plant-adjacent routes moves her estimate by less than two points.

The exchange is unusually polite for economics, and both parties concede the same thing. Fare-free transit has been adopted in dozens of cities and measured carefully in almost none of them, which is why one county's buses have been argued over for four years.

Most mornings the sea off northern Chile sends a wall of grey up the flank of Cerro Pelado. Fishermen have called it the camanchaca for as long as anyone can remember: a fog thick enough to soak a shirt, thin enough to see the sun through. It carries no rain. The village of Aguada, four hundred meters below the ridge, receives less than fifteen millimeters of rain a year and has no river, so for a century its water arrived by truck. In 2019 a research station on the ridge strung forty nets of fine polypropylene mesh across the fog's path. Droplets caught in the mesh, ran down into gutters, and fell through a pipeline to the village tanks.

The station has weighed the catch every day since. The record shows a steady slide. In 2019 the array delivered about 6,900 liters on an average day; by 2025 the same forty nets delivered about 4,100, a loss of two liters in every five. The decline appeared in every month of the fog season, and no single year stands out as unusual — each simply came in below the one before it.

Rosa Iturra, who has run the station since it opened, is careful to say that six years is a short record. Still, she thinks the cause is legible. A warmer ocean surface has pushed the top of the fog layer upward, and the camanchaca now spends more hours drifting above the nets than through them; her instruments put the layer's base an average of thirty meters higher than in 2019. The comparison she trusts most is Cerro Bravo, a ridge twelve kilometers south whose nets sit three hundred meters higher. Cerro Bravo's yield has not fallen. The fog, she says, has not left; it has climbed.

What to do about it is a separate question. Iturra has asked the region for money to rebuild the array two hundred meters upslope, where the layer's new base sits, and the village council has voted to apply. She is blunt about what the move buys: nets on higher ground would return Aguada to its 2019 catch, but if the layer keeps rising at thirty meters every six years, the village will be climbing the ridge again within a generation. Aguada, she says, can stay ahead of the fog for a while — it cannot stay level with it.

Most mornings the sea off northern Chile sends a wall of grey up the flank of Cerro Pelado. Fishermen have called it the camanchaca for as long as anyone can remember: a fog thick enough to soak a shirt, thin enough to see the sun through. It carries no rain. The village of Aguada, four hundred meters below the ridge, receives less than fifteen millimeters of rain a year and has no river, so for a century its water arrived by truck. In 2019 a research station on the ridge strung forty nets of fine polypropylene mesh across the fog's path. Droplets caught in the mesh, ran down into gutters, and fell through a pipeline to the village tanks.

The station has weighed the catch every day since. The record shows a climb that stopped. Daily yield rose from about 3,600 liters in 2019 to about 6,800 in 2022, then held within a few hundred liters of that figure for three straight years. Nothing in the later record moves by much; the line simply flattens after 2022 and stays there, season after season.

The early climb was the crew learning the equipment — tighter mesh tension, a salt rinse every ninth day — and by 2022 those gains were spent. The nets now strip nearly all the water the passing fog will give up, and her sensors find the air leaving the array almost as dry as the mesh can make it. The comparison she trusts most is Cerro Bravo, a ridge twelve kilometers south with identical mesh. It flattened at the same efficiency. The nets, she says, are not being starved; they are full.

She is blunt about what the rows buy: because each net already works at its limit, added nets should add water almost in proportion, so a doubled array ought roughly to double the catch. Aguada, she says, can have as much water as it can afford in mesh — it cannot get more from the mesh it has.

Miss Arden taught ninth-grade composition in a room whose radiator knocked all winter, and she never apologized for the noise. She was not warm. She did not learn our names until October, and when she used mine it landed like a fact, not a greeting. What she had instead was exactness: she would stop mid-sentence, look at the ceiling, and begin the sentence again with one word changed.

In March she told us to keep a notebook — not a journal, she was firm about that, but a record of sentences we could not account for. I filled mine with the talk of the men at my father's garage, and one long entry, four pages, about the way my grandmother said goodbye on the telephone. I knew it was the only good thing I had made.

She gave the notebook back on Monday with nothing written in it — no check, no line, no comment, only a paperclip holding open the page about the telephone. I turned every leaf twice looking for ink. For three weeks I decided she had found nothing there worth the trouble of a pencil, and I stopped writing in the notebook altogether; the blankness felt like a verdict too polite to argue with.

I did not ask her about it for a long time. When I finally did, she was erasing the board and did not turn around.

"I mark what a writer can still repair by Friday," she said. "That page cannot be repaired by Friday. It needs a year and a colder eye, and a pencil of mine on it now would only teach you to want my pencil." Then she asked whether I had kept writing, and I lied and said yes.

Nineteen years later the school dedicated a new library, and I went out of a vanity I would not have admitted to. Miss Arden had died the previous spring. Her sister Nell was handing out programs by the door, and when I told her whose class I had been in she steered me to the window.

Miss Arden had copied my telephone page into a notebook of her own, Nell said, and kept it in a folder she labelled Not Yet — student pages she had refused to mark, reread every summer for thirty years. Standing at that window I understood that the blank margins had not been a verdict but a form of waiting, and that I had spent three weeks reading attention as indifference because indifference was the easier thing to believe. I have been wrong about silence often since.

When the Halvorsen Maritime Museum accepted the Ruvo bequest in 2019, it received nine wooden crates and one typed page. The page said that the crates held fourteen hundred glass-plate negatives made by Elsa Ruvo, who had photographed the working harbor at Sitka Bay between 1908 and 1934, and that the family wished them kept together. Nadia Ochoa, the museum's only conservator, spent that November opening the crates one at a time on a table by the window.

What she found in the fourth crate changed the project. Ruvo had worked fast and cheaply, and on plate after plate she had cut short the last chemical bath, the one that washes away the salts a developed image no longer needs. The plates had never been fixed. Held up to the window, the older exposures showed a faint amber veil creeping in from the edges, and Ochoa understood that every hour of ordinary daylight was still, slowly, printing them darker.

The remedy is not mysterious. A plate in that condition can be rebathed and rewashed, and the image beneath the veil holds. But rebathing must be done one plate at a time by a laboratory equipped for it, and the nearest such laboratory is a private firm in Tacoma whose quote for the fourteen hundred plates came to more than the museum spends on everything in a year. The board read the quote twice and set it down.

So Ochoa proposed the opposite of restoration. Working in a room lit only by a safelight, she and two volunteers photographed each plate at high resolution, one evening at a time, and returned it at once to a lightproof box. By spring the harbor existed as a set of files, and the files were the version the public would see.

The crates now sit in a cold, dark room that no one enters without reason. The plates inside them are still darkening, and the museum has stopped pretending otherwise; what it has saved is the picture, not the glass that carried it.

The page said that the crates held fourteen hundred glass-plate negatives made by Elsa Ruvo, who had photographed the working harbor at Sitka Bay between 1908 and 1934, and that the family wished them kept together. The harbor gallery opened that summer with facsimiles on every wall, well printed and clearly labeled as copies. Sitka Bay can look at its own century, but the century itself is kept two hundred miles from the water it was made on.

variants.passage:
For six seasons Ines Marchetti followed grey chatterbirds through the thorn scrub of the eastern Karoo, and for six seasons one habit refused to make sense. Chatterbirds keep a piercing two-note call for hawks alone; when it sounds, every bird within earshot drops flat or dives into cover, and nobody forages for a minute or more. Yet Marchetti's notebooks filled with hawkless alarms — three hundred and forty of them, by her own count, with nothing overhead but cloud.

Her first thought was ordinary error: a shadow, a startled dove, a bird jumping at nothing. But mistakes ought to be scattered evenly through a group, and these were not. Sixty-nine percent of the hawkless calls came from whichever bird had taken the sentinel perch above the group, the one spot from which the whole foraging party can be watched, and a sentinel has the least excuse for mistaking a shadow.

What followed the calls was just as lopsided. Marchetti filmed fifty-eight hawkless alarms at close range. In forty-one of them the caller dropped from its perch within seconds and carried off the item a startled neighbour had let fall — usually something bulky: a scorpion, a hairless mouse, a beetle grub too fat to swallow whole.

Correlation is not proof, so in her fifth season Marchetti set out to make the alarms happen. On alternate mornings she baited the feeding stations either with slivers of meat that go down in a gulp or with whole scorpions, which a bird must beat and dismember in the open. Hawkless alarms were five times more common on scorpion mornings, and on those mornings the caller finished the meal.

Marchetti now calls the hawkless alarm a lie told for a mouthful: a signal meaning hawk, given by a bird that eats when everyone else believes it. What she cannot explain is why the lie still works. A hundred and forty liars a season ought to have taught the flock to ignore the call, and it has not. Whether the callers hold the trick below some rate at which listeners would stop believing it is the question she means to answer next.

variants.passage:
Coldwater Creek crossed Harbrook for as long as the city had a name, cutting a shallow meander through the flats east of the courthouse. In 1911 the council voted to put it underground.

The reason was disease. The typhoid outbreak of 1909 had killed thirty-one people on the flats, and the county's investigator traced every case to the creek, into which four blocks of privies drained. Burying the water, the council's resolution said, would "remove the source from the reach of the citizen."

The work took nineteen months. Crews laid a barrel of hard-fired brick, four rings thick and nine feet across, for one and a quarter miles, and backfilled the old channel with cinders from the gasworks. The creek did not stop running; it stopped being visible. Within a decade the city's maps no longer drew it, and the street grid crossed the old meander as though the ground there had always been flat. Harbrook's public works ledger names the barrel only twice between 1930 and 1998, each time as a line item for clearing a grate.

The silence ended in 2019, when the city engineer, Nadia Ferrar, sent a camera crawler the length of the barrel — the first full inspection on record.

The barrel itself was strong. Ferrar's crawler found the brick rings sound along nearly their whole length. The mortar was not. At more than two hundred joints the creek was leaking outward into the gravel, and samples drawn from the shallow wells at Beckman School, ninety feet off the barrel's line, carried the same bacterial signature as the water inside it. The pipe built to keep the creek away from people was quietly handing it back to them.

Ferrar's report circulated for four years. Four factions formed in the council chamber: one for repair, one for enlargement, one for removal, one for waiting, each with a cost estimate and a constituency.

In March 2023 they chose repair: $6.8 million to line the barrel from within with a cured-in-place resin sleeve, sealing every joint without opening a single street, across three construction seasons. The creek would stay buried and stay separate — which was, after all, the only thing the city had ever asked of it.

Ferrar's model showed the barrel running full and surcharging at the twenty-year storm, pushing water back up into the basements above it.
